newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Row with China over islands tragic -Philippines.
newsitem.headline: Row with China over islands tragic -Philippines.

text.p: Growing rancour between the Philippines and China over obscure islands in the South China Sea is turning into a tragedy, a senior Philippine official said on Thursday.

The question of who owns the Spratlys and other disputed islands in the South China Sea may not be resolved in anyone's lifetime but there should be attempts to prevent the bickering getting out of hand, Undersecretary for Foreign Affairs, Rodolfo Severino told reporters.
"Our relations with China are actually very good. That is why this is almost...in the nature of a tragedy," he said. "It's a pity because we do have very extensive relations."

No sooner had his news conference finished in Manila than a Chinese official in Beijing raised the temperature by demanding the Philippines stop at once all activity on a tiny cluster of rocks both claim.
The apparently insignificant rock formation called the Scarborugh Shoal is barely visible at high tide and of no obvious commercial value.
On Wednesday, Philippine President Fidel Ramos rejected China's claim to the rocks, which military officials in Manila say are little more than a haven for smugglers.
Last month, Philippine fishermen hoisted their national flag on the rocks where a few days later Manila-based congressmen held a news conference to press the country's claim.
China claims what it calls the Huang Yan islands as historically Beijing's territory.
The squabble follows what Manila said was the intrusion by Chinese naval ships in the Spratly Islands which it claims and which are well south of Scarborough Shoal.
Beijing, which insists all the Spratlys also belong to it, says they were scientific ships on a research mission.
Vietnam, Malaysia, Taiwan and Brunei also claim ownership of some or all the islands.
Speaking during a visit to Hong Kong on Thursday, Ramos said the South China Sea had become a flashpoint in ties with Beijing, but that agreements had been set up to cool tensions.
"We have established our position, they have established their position and we have a mechanism for discussing the subject," he said.
The Spratlys issue was likely to come up in senior official talks between the two sides in Beijing next week, Severino said.
"I don't think we can settle this dispute in our lifetime, but we can at least agree modes on behaviour that would reduce irritations," he said.
One analyst said China was deliberately stirring the issue to test the resolve of the seven-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

"I think what China is doing is probing to what extent the coherence and cohesion (of ASEAN) will remain...ASEAN should signal to China that ASEAN is so important to all the individual countries that they are prepared to challenge China," Carolina Hernandez, president of the Philippine Institute for Strategic abd Development Studies, said.

"(China) wants to be in as many strategic posts (in the South China Sea) as possible, and Vietnam is the only one that will fight them," she added when asked why Beijing appeared to be picking on Manila.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
